# NGS panel scope

This file defines the gene-level scope of the laboratory NGS panel used by this workflow.
It intentionally does not encode transcript, exon, or amplicon numbers.

## Negative-result semantics

When the patient NGS result is explicitly complete, a listed panel gene that is absent from the detected-variant list is interpreted as **no SNV, short insertion/deletion, or short-range complex variant detected in that gene within the validated assay scope**.

Use this negative result when applying diagnostic, prognostic, biomarker, treatment, germline, and other reporting rules. Do not treat the gene as unresolved merely because it is not individually listed in the patient result.

This inference is limited to the assay scope. It does not establish whole-gene biological wild type and does not exclude copy-number changes, rearrangements, structural variants, or other variant classes unless the patient result or another supplied test explicitly assesses them.

If the patient NGS result is described as partial, selected, limited, abbreviated, pending, or otherwise incomplete, do not infer a negative result for an unlisted panel gene.

diagnosis_evidence_cards.interpretation: According to WHO-HAEM5, B-ALL with BCR::ABL1 fusion, KMT2A rearrangement, ETV6::RUNX1 fusion, TCF3::PBX1 fusion, and IGH::IL3 fusion are genetically defined B-ALL entities.
In suspected primary myelofibrosis, detection of ASXL1, EZH2, IDH1, IDH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, or TET2 mutation can support the clonal nature of disease when canonical MPN-driver mutations are absent.

According to the ICC, chronic neutrophilic leukemia requires neutrophilic leukocytosis with segmented/band neutrophils >=80%, neutrophil precursors <10%, monocytes <10%, no significant dysgranulopoiesis, and hypercellular marrow with increased normally maturing neutrophil granulocytes; exclusion of BCR::ABL1-positive CML, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, primary myelofibrosis, and myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and TK fusions; and either CSF3R T618I/another activating CSF3R mutation or, if CSF3R is absent, persistent neutrophilia for >=3 months with splenomegaly and no reactive cause (with myeloid clonality demonstrated if a plasma-cell neoplasm is present). The WBC threshold is >=13 x 10^9/L with an activating CSF3R mutation and >=25 x 10^9/L without one; absence of CSF3R does not exclude CNL.
In myeloproliferative neoplasm, unclassifiable (MPN-U), ASXL1, EZH2, IDH1, IDH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, or TET2 mutations detected by sensitive molecular methods can support the clonal nature of disease.

According to the ICC, atypical chronic myeloid leukemia (aCML) requires WBC >=13 x 10^9/L due to neutrophils and precursors with promyelocytes/myelocytes/metamyelocytes >=10%; cytopenia using MDS thresholds; <20% blasts; prominent dysgranulopoiesis; monocytes <10% and eosinophils <10% of leukocytes; hypercellular marrow with granulocytic proliferation/dysplasia; and absence of BCR::ABL1 and TK-fusion myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms. Absence of JAK2, CALR, and MPL supports the diagnosis, and SETBP1 mutation, often with ASXL1, provides additional support.
Detection of a CSF3R mutation in suspected atypical chronic myeloid leukemia (aCML) should prompt careful morphologic review to exclude chronic neutrophilic leukemia.

According to the ICC, MDS/MPN with i(17q) is a provisional subtype of MDS/MPN, NOS. Diagnosis requires leukocytosis >=13 x 10^9/L, cytopenia using MDS thresholds, <20% blasts in blood and bone marrow, dysgranulopoiesis with nonsegmented or pseudo-Pelger-Huet neutrophils, and i(17q) either isolated or with one additional abnormality other than -7/del(7q). BCR::ABL1, myeloid/lymphoid-neoplasm tyrosine-kinase gene fusions, and JAK2/CALR/MPL mutations should be absent, and recent cytotoxic or growth-factor therapy must not explain the phenotype. SRSF2 and SETBP1 co-mutations further support the diagnosis.

According to the ICC, MDS with mutated SF3B1 requires SF3B1 mutation VAF >=10%, at least one cytopenia, no ICC-defined cytosis at diagnosis, <5% marrow blasts and <2% blood blasts, and absence of multihit TP53, RUNX1 mutation, isolated del(5q), -7/del(7q), 3q26.2 abnormalities, and complex karyotype. Dysplasia is typically present but is not required, and ring sideroblasts are not required.
AML with mutated TP53 is defined by >=20% marrow or blood blasts, or pure erythroid leukemia, plus any somatic TP53 mutation with VAF >10%; monoallelic TP53 mutations are allowed.
In germline RUNX1-, ANKRD26-, or ETV6-associated constitutional platelet disorders, marrow megakaryocytic dysplasia can be present with isolated thrombocytopenia in the absence of MDS.
According to the ICC, acute promyelocytic leukemia with PML::RARA can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts.
According to the ICC, APL with other RARA rearrangements can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts; listed RARA partners include IRF2BP2, NPM1, ZBTB16, STAT5B, STAT3, TBL1XR1, FIP1L1, and BCOR.
According to the ICC, AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1, CBFB::MYH11, MLLT3::KMT2A, or DEK::NUP214 can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts.
According to the ICC, AML with other KMT2A rearrangements can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts; listed partners include AFF1, AFDN, MLLT10, TET1, ELL, and MLLT1.
According to the ICC, AML with inv(3) or t(3;3) involving GATA2 and MECOM can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts.
According to the ICC, AML with other MECOM rearrangements can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts; listed examples include MECOM rearrangements involving MYC, ETV6, or RUNX1.
According to the ICC, AML with BCR::ABL1 requires >=20% blasts.
The ICC does not use the MDS/AML category for BCR::ABL1-positive AML because of overlap with progression of BCR::ABL1-positive CML.
According to the ICC, AML with mutated NPM1 can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts.
According to the ICC, AML with an in-frame bZIP CEBPA mutation can be diagnosed with >=10% blasts, without requiring biallelic CEBPA mutations.
According to the ICC, MDS/AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations has 10%-19% blasts and is defined by mutation in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2.
According to the ICC, AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations requires >=20% blasts and is defined by mutation in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2.

After excluding TP53 mutation, myelodysplasia-related gene mutation, and other class-defining recurring genetic abnormalities, AML with myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormalities is defined at >=20% blasts by specified abnormalities including complex karyotype, del/t/add(5q), -7/del(7q), +8, del/t/add(12p), i(17q), -17/add(17p)/del(17p), del(20q), or idic(X)(q13).
AML, NOS requires >=20% blasts after excluding class-defining genetic categories.
Myeloid sarcoma remains an ICC AML-related disease category and does not require a marrow or blood blast-percentage threshold for its classification.

For AML categories with listed recurrent genetic abnormalities other than BCR::ABL1 and the remaining >=20%-blast categories, the ICC permits AML diagnosis with at least 10% blasts or blast equivalents.
Single-gene mutation or gene-fusion AML categories take precedence over myelodysplasia-related gene-mutation and myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic groups.
When TP53 mutation overlaps another AML genetic category, the ICC states that the TP53 mutation should be noted with the other genetic abnormality.
Pure erythroid leukemia is typically TP53-mutated and is classified within AML with TP53 mutation in the ICC.
According to the ICC, therapy-related status is a diagnostic qualifier appended to the specific AML or MDS/AML diagnosis rather than a stand-alone AML disease category.
According to the ICC, progression from a confirmed prior MDS is a diagnostic qualifier appended to the specific AML or MDS/AML diagnosis.
According to the ICC, progression from a confirmed prior MDS/MPN is a diagnostic qualifier appended to the specific AML or MDS/AML diagnosis, with the antecedent MDS/MPN specified.
Underlying germline predisposition is used as a qualifier following the specific AML or MDS/AML diagnosis.
The ICC recognizes ETV6::RUNX1, IL3::IGH, and TCF3::PBX1 B-ALL as recurrent-genetic-abnormality subtypes.
ETV6::RUNX1-like B-ALL is a provisional ICC entity defined by an ETV6::RUNX1-like gene-expression/phenotypic profile despite lacking the canonical structural lesion.
The Nordic 2019 guidelines list germline predisposition involving CEBPA, DDX41, RUNX1, ANKRD26, ETV6, GATA2, SAMD9, SAMD9L, SRP72, CBL, KRAS, NF1, PTPN11, TP53, and MECOM as autosomal dominant.
According to the Nordic 2019 guidelines, germline RUNX1 predisposition is associated with MDS and AML, with ALL also listed, and has a reported lifetime myeloid-malignancy risk of approximately 45%.

According to the Nordic 2019 guidelines, severe congenital neutropenia associated with ELANE, CSF3R, GFI1, SRP54, HAX1, G6PC3, JAGN1, VPS45, or WAS predisposes to MDS and AML, with a reported lifetime myeloid-malignancy risk of 21–40%.
Poor stem-cell mobilisation in a sibling donor candidate is a clinical clue to hereditary myeloid predisposition and has been reported in rare cases with germline TERC and RUNX1 variants.

In patients with MDS or AML, a RUNX1, GATA2, TP53, ETV6, or CEBPA variant detected on a somatic NGS panel at VAF 40–60% or >90% can suggest germline origin; the Nordic 2019 guidelines recommend confirmation in extra-haematological tissue after consent.
Asymptomatic carriers of germline RUNX1, ANKRD26, or ETV6 variants may have thrombocytopenia or a bleeding tendency at baseline, including bleeding tendency without thrombocytopenia.

Under the 2022 International Consensus Classification (ICC), PML::RARA, RUNX1::RUNX1T1, CBFB::MYH11, MLLT3::KMT2A, DEK::NUP214, inv(3)/t(3;3) involving GATA2 and MECOM, mutated NPM1, and in-frame bZIP CEBPA mutations are AML-defining recurrent abnormalities at ≥10% blasts; BCR::ABL1 requires ≥20% blasts because of overlap with chronic myeloid leukemia.

Under the 2022 ICC, IRF2BP2::RARA, NPM1::RARA, ZBTB16::RARA, STAT5B::RARA, STAT3::RARA, TBL1XR1::RARA, FIP1L1::RARA, and BCOR::RARA are recognized recurring RARA-rearranged APL entities and, as AML-defining recurrent abnormalities other than BCR::ABL1, establish AML/APL at ≥10% blasts.
Under the 2022 ICC, AFF1::KMT2A, AFDN::KMT2A, MLLT10::KMT2A, TET1::KMT2A, KMT2A::ELL, and KMT2A::MLLT1 are recognized recurring KMT2A-rearranged AML entities and establish AML at ≥10% blasts.
Under the 2022 ICC, t(2;3) involving MECOM, MYC/MECOM t(3;8), ETV6::MECOM, and MECOM::RUNX1 are recognized recurring MECOM-rearranged AML entities and establish AML at ≥10% blasts.

Under the 2022 ICC, PRDM16::RPN1, RBM15::MRTFA, NPM1::MLF1, NUP98::NSD1, ETV6::MNX1, KAT6A::CREBBP, PICALM::MLLT10, NUP98::KMD5A, FUS::ERG, RUNX1::CBFA2T3, CBFA2T3::GLIS2, and other NUP98 rearrangements are listed as rare recurring AML-defining genetic entities and establish AML at ≥10% blasts.

Under the 2022 ICC, when higher-priority recurrent AML-defining abnormalities are absent, a pathogenic somatic TP53 mutation with variant allele fraction ≥10%, with or without loss of the wild-type allele, defines TP53-mutated AML at ≥20% blasts; the corresponding 10%-19% blast category is MDS/AML.

Under the 2022 ICC, when higher-priority recurrent AML-defining abnormalities and TP53-mutated disease are absent, pathogenic mutations in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2 define AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations at ≥20% blasts, irrespective of prior MDS; the corresponding 10%-19% blast category is MDS/AML.

Under the 2022 ICC, when higher-priority AML-defining categories are absent, del(5q)/t(5q)/add(5q), monosomy 7/del(7q), trisomy 8, del(12p)/t(12p)/add(12p), i(17q), monosomy 17/add(17p)/del(17p), del(20q), idic(X)(q13), or a complex karyotype of ≥3 unrelated chromosome abnormalities (excluding hyperdiploid karyotypes with ≥3 trisomies/polysomies and no structural abnormality) defines AML with myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormality at ≥20% blasts and MDS/AML at 10%-19% blasts.

Under the 2022 ICC, prior chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or immune intervention for a nonmyeloid neoplasm is recorded as a therapy-related diagnostic qualifier to the genetically defined AML category rather than as a separate AML entity.
Under the 2022 ICC, a prior MDS is appended as a diagnostic qualifier to the AML category only when it was established by standard diagnostics more than 3 months before AML diagnosis.

Under the 2022 ICC, the AML classification hierarchy is: recurrent AML-defining genetic abnormality first; otherwise TP53-mutated AML; otherwise AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations; otherwise AML with myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormalities.
Germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic RUNX1, ANKRD26, and ETV6 variants are recognized myeloid-neoplasm predisposition disorders associated with a preexisting platelet disorder.
Under the 2022 ICC, the former AML with myelodysplasia-related changes (AML-MRC) category is removed, and multilineage dysplasia is no longer an independent criterion for that AML category.

Under the 2022 ICC, cases lacking a recurrent AML-defining abnormality, TP53-mutated category, myelodysplasia-related gene mutation category, or myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic category are classified as AML, not otherwise specified at ≥20% blasts, or MDS/AML at 10%-19% blasts, irrespective of multilineage dysplasia.
Under the 2022 ICC, when an inherited germline predisposing disorder is identified in a patient with AML, the germline disorder is appended as a diagnostic qualifier to the specific AML category.
Under the 2022 ICC, BCR::ABL1-positive disease with 10%-19% blasts is classified as chronic myeloid leukemia in accelerated phase rather than AML.

Under the 2022 ICC, in a patient with a history of chronic myeloid leukemia, BCR::ABL1-positive disease with ≥20% blasts is classified as CML in myeloid blast phase rather than de novo AML with BCR::ABL1.

Under the 2022 ICC, a prior MDS/MPN is appended as a diagnostic qualifier to the AML category only when the MDS/MPN was established by standard diagnostics more than 3 months before AML diagnosis, and the MDS/MPN type should be specified.
Under the 2022 ICC, myeloblasts, monoblasts, and megakaryoblasts are included in the blast count used for AML classification.
Under the 2022 ICC, in AML with monocytic or myelomonocytic differentiation, monoblasts and promonocytes are counted as blast equivalents, whereas abnormal monocytes are not.
Under the 2022 ICC, in PML::RARA or variant RARA-rearranged APL/AML, promyelocytes are counted as blast equivalents for classification.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, a 20% blast cutoff is retained to delineate MDS from AML, but most AML types with defining genetic abnormalities may be diagnosed below 20% blasts. AML with BCR::ABL1 and AML with CEBPA mutation remain exceptions requiring ≥20% blasts. When a genetically defined AML is diagnosed below 20%, morphologic and molecular findings must be correlated to establish that the defining abnormality is driving the disease.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML is organized into two families: AML with defining genetic abnormalities and AML defined by differentiation. The term AML, NOS is no longer applied to the differentiation-defined family.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with PML::RARA, RUNX1::RUNX1T1, CBFB::MYH11, DEK::NUP214 or RBM15::MRTFA is classified as AML with a defining genetic abnormality.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with BCR::ABL1 requires ≥20% blasts, principally to avoid overlap with CML.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with CEBPA mutation includes either biallelic CEBPA mutations or a single CEBPA mutation in the basic leucine zipper region and requires ≥20% blasts.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with KMT2A, MECOM or NUP98 rearrangement may be diagnosed with <20% blasts.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with NPM1 mutation may be diagnosed irrespective of blast count, with judicious clinicopathologic correlation.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, somatic RUNX1 mutation does not define a standalone AML type because it lacks sufficient specificity across defining molecular contexts.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML, myelodysplasia-related (AML-MR; formerly AML with myelodysplasia-related changes) requires ≥20% blasts with a myeloid immunophenotype plus at least one qualifying MDS-related feature: a history of MDS or MDS/MPN; a defining somatic mutation in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1 or ZRSR2; or a defining cytogenetic abnormality comprising complex karyotype (≥3 abnormalities), 5q deletion/loss, monosomy 7 or 7q deletion/loss, 11q deletion, 12p deletion/loss, monosomy 13 or 13q deletion, 17p deletion/loss, isochromosome 17q or idic(X)(q13). Morphologic dysplasia alone is insufficient. A diagnosis of acute erythroid leukaemia supersedes AML-MR.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with minimal differentiation requires blasts negative (<3%) for MPO and SBB by cytochemistry and expression of at least two myeloid-associated antigens such as CD13, CD33 and CD117. It also requires ≥20% blasts, absence of a defining genetic AML type, absence of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, absence of myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy and no prior MPN.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML without maturation requires ≥3% blasts positive for MPO or SBB, NSE negativity, <10% maturing granulocytic cells and expression of at least two myeloid-associated antigens. It also requires ≥20% blasts, absence of a defining genetic AML type, absence of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, absence of myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy and no prior MPN.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with maturation requires ≥3% blasts positive for MPO or SBB, ≥10% maturing granulocytic cells, <20% monocyte-lineage cells and expression of at least two myeloid-associated antigens. It also requires ≥20% blasts, absence of a defining genetic AML type, absence of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, absence of myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy and no prior MPN.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, acute basophilic leukaemia requires basophilic blasts/immature or mature basophils with metachromasia on toluidine blue, blasts negative for MPO, SBB and NSE, and absence of strong CD117-equivalent expression. It also requires ≥20% blasts, absence of a defining genetic AML type, absence of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, absence of myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy and no prior MPN.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, acute myelomonocytic leukaemia requires ≥20% monocytes and precursors, ≥20% maturing granulocytic cells and ≥3% blasts positive for MPO. It also requires ≥20% blasts, absence of a defining genetic AML type, absence of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, absence of myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy and no prior MPN.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, acute monocytic leukaemia requires ≥80% monocytes and/or their precursors, <20% maturing granulocytic cells, and blasts/promonocytes expressing at least two monocytic markers among CD11c, CD14, CD36 and CD64 or showing NSE positivity. It also requires ≥20% blasts, absence of a defining genetic AML type, absence of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, absence of myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy and no prior MPN.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, acute erythroid leukaemia is characterized by erythroid predominance, usually ≥80% of marrow cellularity, with ≥30% proerythroblasts; cases with <80% erythroid cellularity are recognized when they share the same clinicopathologic features. “Pure erythroid leukaemia” is retained as an acceptable related term. The other shared differentiation-defined AML exclusions apply, but the ≥20% blast requirement does not.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia requires blasts expressing at least one platelet glycoprotein marker—CD41, CD61 or CD42b. It also requires ≥20% blasts, absence of a defining genetic AML type, absence of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, absence of myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy and no prior MPN.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML with other defined genetic alterations provides a classification category for uncommon or emerging genetically defined AML subtypes, including rare genetic fusions; CBFA2T3::GLIS2 is recognized in this category in the acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia context.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, a myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy (MN-pCT) is diagnosed when criteria for AML, MDS or MDS/MPN are fulfilled in a patient with a documented history of chemotherapy or large-field radiation therapy for an unrelated neoplasm. CCUS is excluded. NPM1-mutated disease and core-binding-factor leukaemias with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 or CBFB::MYH11 still receive the post-cytotoxic designation when the exposure history is present. PARP1 inhibitors qualify as an exposure and methotrexate does not. The specific myeloid diagnosis should be given when possible with “post cytotoxic therapy” appended.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, “AML with KMT2A rearrangement” replaces the former term “AML with t(9;11)(p22;q23); KMT2A-MLLT3.”
A RUNX1 or TP53 variant detected in hematopoietic tissue should not be assumed to be germline or somatic based on the variant itself, because variants in either gene can occur in both settings.
In unexplained cytopenia, SF3B1 mutation strongly supports an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype, including when SF3B1 is the only detected mutation.
In unexplained cytopenia, SRSF2, U2AF1, ZRSR2, JAK2, or RUNX1 mutation strongly supports an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype, whether detected alone or with other mutations.

In unexplained cytopenia, an isolated TET2, DNMT3A, or ASXL1 mutation provides substantially less support for an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype, than the same mutation occurring with additional genetic lesions.
In unexplained cytopenia, TP53 mutation is more supportive of an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype, when co-mutated—most often with TET2 or ASXL1—than when TP53 is isolated.

In unexplained cytopenia, co-mutation patterns in which TET2, DNMT3A, or ASXL1 co-occurs with RUNX1, EZH2, CBL, TP53, NRAS, CUX1, or IDH2 are highly predictive of an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype.

In unexplained cytopenia, SF3B1 mutation is highly specific for a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplasia—MDS, MDS/MPN, or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes—even when SF3B1 is the only detected mutation.
In unexplained cytopenia, ZRSR2 mutation is highly specific for a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplasia—MDS, MDS/MPN, or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes.

In unexplained cytopenia, co-mutation patterns in which TET2, ASXL1, or DNMT3A co-occurs with RUNX1, EZH2, CBL, BCOR, CUX1, TP53, IDH1, or IDH2 are highly specific for a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplasia—MDS, MDS/MPN, or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes.

In unexplained cytopenia, SRSF2 or U2AF1 mutation is highly specific for a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplasia—MDS, MDS/MPN, or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes—except when co-occurring with JAK2 in primary myelofibrosis.

In patients with CCUS and inconclusive dysplasia, the authors propose that highly specific mutation patterns—SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2 mutation, or TET2, ASXL1, or DNMT3A co-mutated with RUNX1, EZH2, CBL, BCOR, CUX1, TP53, IDH1, or IDH2—may provide presumptive evidence of MDS even when definitive morphologic criteria are absent.

In TP53-mutated AML/MDS, findings supporting multihit TP53 status include TP53 cnLOH demonstrated by dedicated testing; loss of chromosome 17 or 17p; two or more TP53 mutations; or a single TP53 mutation with VAF >55% and sequencing coverage >200×. A TP53 VAF <55% does not exclude multihit disease.

In TP53-mutated AML/MDS, complex karyotype may suggest multihit TP53 status but is an imperfect surrogate: some TP53-mutated cases with complex karyotype lack chromosome 17 deletion or TP53 cnLOH, whereas some cases with TP53 cnLOH have noncomplex karyotypes.
